title: "From a research question to a gene set: liver fibrosis"
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 150,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
```

AOP-Wiki is published as RDF and is normally queried with SPARQL. That is a
barrier for some people, and it means that questions which are conceptually
simple ("which genes belong to this Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP)?") require a
query language.

This article answers one such question end to end, using only R4AOP functions.
The question is:

> Which Adverse Outcome Pathways describe liver fibrosis, how is one of them
> structured, and which genes are linked to it?

```{r setup}
library(R4AOP)
library(ggplot2)
```

## 1. Find the relevant pathways

`aop_list()` retrieves AOPs and accepts a free-text filter, which searches the
AOP title and short name.

```{r find}
fibrosis <- aop_list(q = "liver fibrosis")
fibrosis[, c("id", "title", "oecd_status")]
```

The result is an ordinary tibble, so the returned set can be narrowed by any
column, according to the context of the question. Development stage, last
modification date, or the identifiers of the events a pathway contains are all
available:

```{r filtering}
# by development stage
fibrosis[which(fibrosis$oecd_status == "WPHA/WNT Endorsed"), c("id", "title")]

# by recency of curation
fibrosis[fibrosis$modified > "2023-01-01", c("id", "title", "modified")]
```

AOPs are living documents: most are still under development and are revised as
evidence accumulates, so no single column defines a "correct" subset. Which
filter is appropriate depends on the question being asked. Here we continue with
OECD endorsed AOP:

```{r pick}
aop_id <- 38
aop_id
```

The `mie_ids` and `ao_ids` columns hold identifiers rather than text. Setting
`resolve_titles = TRUE` looks those up, so the start and end points of each
pathway can be read directly:

```{r resolve-titles}
titled <- aop_list(q = "liver fibrosis", resolve_titles = TRUE)

data.frame(
  id  = titled$id,
  mie = vapply(titled$mie_titles, function(x) paste(x, collapse = "; "), ""),
  ao  = vapply(titled$ao_titles,  function(x) paste(x, collapse = "; "), "")
)
```

## 2. Inspect the structure of the pathway

A single AOP record gives the descriptive metadata.

```{r single-aop}
aop <- aop_get(aop_id)
aop$title
aop$oecd_status
```

Its Key Events are the biological steps of the pathway. The `role` column marks
where each event is positioned in the cause-and-effect chain: `mie` is the molecular initiating event, `ao` the adverse
outcome, and `ke` everything in between.

```{r key-events}
kes <- aop_key_events(aop_id)
kes[, c("id", "title", "role")]
```

```{r roles}
table(kes$role)
```

The Key Event Relationships are the directed links between those steps. Each
relationship carries the upstream (cause) and downstream (effect) Key Event.

```{r kers}
kers <- aop_kers(aop_id)

edges <- data.frame(
  ker_id = kers$id,
  from   = kers$upstream$title,
  to     = kers$downstream$title
)
edges
```

Read together, `kes` and `edges` are the full topology of the pathway: nodes and
directed edges. Everything needed to build a graph object or a diagram is
already here, in two calls.

## 3. Retrieve the linked genes

AOP-Wiki genes come from the enriched RDF layer, which links genes to Key Events
and to Key Event Relationships. The `detected_by` column records how the link
was made: `regex` for pattern matching, `ner` for named entity recognition, and
`both` where the two methods agree.

```{r genes}
genes <- aop_genes(aop_id)
nrow(genes)
head(genes)
```

```{r by-method}
table(genes$detected_by)
```

The three groups are not equally trustworthy. Genes found by both methods are
the most conservative set; genes found by a single method are broader but
noisier. Making that distinction visible is the point of keeping the column.

```{r fig-methods, fig.cap = "Distinct genes per detection method."}
per_method <- aggregate(symbol ~ detected_by, data = genes,
                        FUN = function(x) length(unique(x)))
names(per_method)[2] <- "n_genes"

ggplot(per_method, aes(x = reorder(detected_by, n_genes), y = n_genes)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1F4E79", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n_genes), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Detection method", y = "Distinct genes") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## 4. Genes per Key Event

Because each gene record names the entity it was linked to, gene sets can be
built per Key Event rather than for the pathway as a whole. This is what makes
the data usable for transcriptomics: each Key Event becomes a candidate gene
set.

```{r ke-genes}
ke_genes <- merge(
  genes[genes$entity_type == "key_event", ],
  data.frame(entity_id = kes$id, ke_title = kes$title, role = kes$role),
  by = "entity_id"
)

ke_counts <- aggregate(symbol ~ ke_title + detected_by, data = ke_genes,
                       FUN = function(x) length(unique(x)))
names(ke_counts)[3] <- "n_genes"
head(ke_counts)
```

```{r fig-ke, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Genes linked to each Key Event, split by detection method."}
ggplot(ke_counts, aes(x = reorder(ke_title, n_genes), y = n_genes,
                      fill = detected_by)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(both = "#1F4E79", ner = "#7FA8C9",
                               regex = "#C9D9E8")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Distinct genes", fill = "Detected by") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

A gene set for one Key Event, ready for enrichment analysis, is then one line:

```{r gene-set}
mie_id <- kes$id[kes$role == "mie"]
mie_genes <- unique(ke_genes$symbol[ke_genes$entity_id == mie_id])
length(mie_genes)
head(mie_genes, 10)
```

## 5. Reproducibility

AOP-Wiki is curated continuously, so results depend on the version of the data
that was queried. Every R4AOP result carries that version, and it can be
reported alongside the findings.

```{r version}
aop_data_version(fibrosis)
```

## 6. What this replaces

Retrieving the same information directly from the RDF endpoint means one SPARQL
query per step: declaring prefixes, matching the AOP to its Key Events through
`aopo:has_key_event`, following `aopo:has_key_event_relationship` for the
topology, and joining the enriched gene links. Each query has to be written
against the RDF schema and kept in step with it, in every project that needs it.

With R4AOP the six steps above are six function calls. The package covers the
routine tasks that most analyses begin with: listing AOPs, filtering them,
following the links to Key Events, Key Event Relationships, stressors,
chemicals and genes, and pulling the results into tibbles that fit directly
into an R workflow. These are the steps that are repeated in nearly every
project, and they are the ones the package makes immediate. SPARQL stays
available for tailored or complex retrieval that no endpoint covers.
